No two edges of one color share a player: round 0 (accent) is A-B and C-D, round 1 (teal) A-C and B-D, and round 2 (violet) A-D and B-C. The card lists the three rounds." width="100%"} An edge coloring gives each edge a color such that the edges meeting at any node all differ. Each color class is then a matching, a set of edges with no node in common, so a coloring with `k` colors splits the edges into `k` rounds that can each run at once: the matches of a round-robin tournament (players are nodes, games are edges), transfers between machines that can each handle one at a time, or wavelengths on the links of an optical network. A node with `d` edges needs `d` different colors around it, so at least $\Delta$ colors are needed, $\Delta$ being the maximum degree. Vizing's theorem says $\Delta + 1$ always suffice, and this method always uses at most $\Delta + 1$ colors, though sometimes one more than the fewest possible (telling which is NP-hard). Edge direction is ignored. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [dict[int, int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Each edge ID mapped to its color, numbered from 0 up to at most $\Delta$, in edge ID order. A graph with no edges gives an empty dictionary. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph has a self-loop or parallel edges (on a directed graph, also both `u -> v` and `v -> u`), for which $\Delta + 1$ colors may not be enough. ::: ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~is_valid_edge_coloring`) : Check an edge coloring. [](`~greedy_color`) : Color the nodes instead. ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} The Misra and Gries (1992) algorithm, a constructive proof of Vizing's theorem. Edges are colored in ID order. An edge whose two ends share a free color takes the lowest one; otherwise the algorithm builds a *fan* of neighbors around one end, swaps two colors along an alternating path, and shifts colors around the fan to free one for the new edge. $O(V E)$ time in the worst case, and close to linear in practice. NetworkX pull request #7397 adds `edge_coloring` with the same $\Delta + 1$ guarantee and an equivalent fan and alternating-path method. Its colorings can differ from these, and it returns `{(u, v): color}` with both orders of every edge, where this returns `{edge_id: color}`. ## Examples {.doc-examples} A round-robin among four players: each of the six games is an edge, and each color a round in which no player plays twice. Three rounds suffice, since each player has three games: ::: {#391eae3b .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec players = ["ann", "bob", "cy", "dee"] g = ec.Graph().add_nodes(players) g.add_edges([(a, b) for i, a in enumerate(players) for b in players[i + 1:]]) label = g.get_label_from_id games = {e: f"{label(u)}-{label(v)}" for e, u, v in g.get_edges_as_tuples()} rounds = {} for edge, color in g.edge_coloring().items(): rounds.setdefault(color, []).append(games[edge]) rounds ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` {0: ['ann-bob', 'cy-dee'], 1: ['ann-cy', 'bob-dee'], 2: ['ann-dee', 'bob-cy']} ``` ::: :::
